| [CLAIM-291](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-291.md) | The adjoint of a square-integrable integral operator is the integral operator with the conjugate-transposed kernel | The record's own step, written down in [THEORY-009](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-009.md) and marked there as not the Riesz article's, which covers matrices and bounded operators only. For a kernel k in L²(μ⊗ν), the operator (Tf)(x) = ∫ k(x,y) f(y) dν(y) from L²(ν) to L²(μ) has adjoint (T*g)(y) = ∫ k̄(x,y) g(x) dμ(x), by Cauchy–Schwarz and Fubini. So T is self-adjoint, when μ = ν, exactly when k(x,y) = k̄(y,x) almost everywhere. It does not say where the symmetry of k comes from, which is [THEORY-009](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-009.md)'s question, and it is not claimed for kernels that are not square-integrable. | Active |

| [CLAIM-378](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-378.md) | A representational similarity index invariant to every invertible linear map depends on a representation only through its column space, so it takes one value on all column-centred representations of rank n − 1, as it does on all representations of rank n | The generalization of [THEORY-236](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-236.md)'s theorem. Since XA always has the column space of X, the GL(p) orbits are exactly the sets of n × p matrices sharing a column space. Theorem 1 is the case of column space ℝⁿ. | [CLAIM-382](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-382.md) | In an autoencoder initialised with i.i.d. Gaussian weights and zero biases and trained by SGD or momentum SGD on a loss of its output, the law of each hidden layer's learned representation is invariant under every orthogonal map of that layer that commutes with its activation, so under a radial activation no basis is privileged in law, while elementwise tanh or Leaky-ReLU yields invariance only under the signed permutations or the permutations, which leaves the standard axes free to be privileged | [THEORY-288](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-288.md)'s symmetry argument, stated as the record's own and proved. Transform the parameters by orthogonal maps Q_l of the hidden spaces that commute with the activation. The network then computes Q_l h_l and the same output, so the loss is invariant. Gradient steps commute with the transformation, and an i.i.d. Gaussian initialisation is invariant under it, so the law of the trained representations is too. For radial activations this is all of O(n), and no basis is privileged in law. For elementwise ones it is a finite group, so the axes may be privileged. Whether they are, and how strongly, is [THEORY-288](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-288.md)'s empirical content. The argument needs an orthogonally equivariant optimiser, and fails for Adam. | Active |
